learn: Historians analyse evidence to explain change and continuity over time.
Primary sources come from the time studied; secondary sources interpret them later.
Sourcing asks who made a source, when, why and for whom.
check: A diary from 1850 is a ___ source.
lessons.try: Source a primary document using the questions who, when, why and for whom.

learn: The first civilizations rose in river valleys: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and China.
Rivers provided water, fertile soil and transport.
These societies developed writing, law, cities and social hierarchy.
check: Which was a river valley civilization?
lessons.try: Compare two river valley civilizations in a chart.

learn: Classical Greece gave democracy and philosophy; Rome gave republican government and law.
Han China and Maurya and Gupta India built large empires with lasting cultures.
Classical empires spread religions and trade over large regions.
lessons.try: Compare the Han and Roman empires.

learn: The Silk Roads linked China, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe.
Indian Ocean trade connected East Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia using monsoon winds.
Trans-Saharan trade moved gold and salt across West Africa.
check: The Silk Roads linked China and...
lessons.try: Map three trade networks and their goods.

learn: Islam spread rapidly from Arabia after 632 across North Africa, Spain and Asia.
Buddhism spread from India to China, Korea and Japan.
Christianity shaped medieval Europe and the Byzantine Empire.
lessons.try: Explain how trade helped spread religions.

learn: The Mongol Empire (1200s) was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
The Pax Mongolica made Silk Road trade safer.
Trade networks also spread the Black Death in the 1300s.
check: The Mongol Empire was the largest ___ empire.
lessons.try: Evaluate the Mongols' positive and negative effects.

units.t: Renaissance, Reformation and the Scientific Revolution

learn: The Renaissance began in Italy in the 1300s, reviving classical learning.
Humanism emphasised human potential and individual achievement.
Gutenberg's printing press (about 1450) spread ideas quickly.
check: The printing press was developed around...
lessons.try: Explain how the printing press changed Europe.

learn: Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) challenged Church practices.
Protestant churches spread across northern Europe.
Religious wars followed, ending with the Peace of Westphalia (1648).
check: The Peace of Westphalia was in...
lessons.try: Analyse the causes of the Reformation.

learn: Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton challenged old ideas with observation and mathematics.
The scientific method emphasised evidence and experiment.
Newton's "Principia" (1687) described universal gravitation.
check: The heliocentric model puts ___ at the centre.
lessons.try: Explain why the heliocentric model was revolutionary.

units.t: Exploration, Empires and the Atlantic World

learn: Motives: wealth, religion and glory; new ship and navigation technology helped.
Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492; da Gama reached India in 1498.
Spain and Portugal divided claims in the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).
check: The Treaty of Tordesillas divided claims between Spain and...
An important navigation tool was the...
lessons.try: Map major voyages of exploration.

learn: Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec (1521) and Inca (1530s) empires.
Diseases like smallpox killed a large majority of Indigenous people in many regions.
Colonial systems like the encomienda forced Indigenous labour.
check: The deadliest factor for Indigenous peoples was...
lessons.try: Analyse why small Spanish forces defeated large empires.

lessons.t: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Columbian Exchange
learn: About 12 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic between the 1500s and 1800s.
The Middle Passage was brutal; many died at sea.
The Columbian Exchange transferred crops, animals and diseases, reshaping diets worldwide.
check: About ___ million Africans were forcibly transported.
Potatoes spread from the Americas through the...
lessons.try: Read a primary account of the Middle Passage and write a reflection.

learn: Locke argued for natural rights; Montesquieu for separation of powers; Rousseau for the social contract.
Voltaire championed freedom of speech and religion.
These ideas challenged absolute monarchy.
lessons.try: Match Enlightenment thinkers to modern rights.

learn: The American Revolution (1775-1783) created a republic based on Enlightenment ideas.
The French Revolution (1789) overthrew the monarchy; the Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed equality.
The Reign of Terror showed how revolutions can turn violent.
check: The Reign of Terror was part of the ___ Revolution.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed...
lessons.try: Compare the American and French revolutions.

learn: The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804), led by Toussaint Louverture, was the only successful large-scale slave revolt.
Simón Bolívar led independence movements in South America.
Mexico gained independence from Spain in 1821.
check: The Haitian Revolution was led by...
lessons.try: Research Toussaint Louverture and present his impact.

learn: Industrialisation began in Britain in the late 1700s with textile machines and steam power.
Factories and railways transformed work and cities.
Urban workers faced long hours, child labour and unsafe conditions.
lessons.try: Analyse a primary source about factory conditions.

learn: Labour unions formed to fight for better wages and conditions.
Reformers passed laws limiting child labour.
Karl Marx criticised capitalism; others defended free markets.
lessons.try: Debate the benefits and costs of industrialisation.

learn: In the late 1800s, European powers colonised most of Africa (the "Scramble for Africa", 1884-1885 Berlin Conference).
Motives: raw materials, markets, national rivalry and racist ideas of superiority.
Colonised peoples resisted, as in Ethiopia's victory at Adwa (1896).
lessons.try: Map colonial Africa in 1914.

units.t: World War I and Its Aftermath

learn: MAIN causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism.
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 triggered the war.
Alliances drew most of Europe into the conflict.
check: The war was triggered by the assassination of...
lessons.try: Make a cause-and-effect diagram of the outbreak of war.

learn: Trench warfare on the Western Front led to stalemate and huge casualties.
New weapons included machine guns, tanks, planes and poison gas.
About 9 million soldiers died.
check: Fighting on the Western Front used...
A new weapon in WWI was the...
lessons.try: Read soldiers' letters from the trenches.

learn: The war ended in 1918; the Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany and imposed reparations.
The League of Nations was created but was weak.
Resentment in Germany helped set the stage for another war.
check: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in...
lessons.try: Evaluate the Treaty of Versailles.

units.t: The Great Depression and World War II

learn: The 1929 stock market crash triggered a worldwide depression.
Unemployment soared; in the US it reached about 25%.
Economic hardship helped extremist movements gain power.
lessons.try: Analyse photographs from the Great Depression.

learn: Totalitarian regimes rose: Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany under Hitler and the Soviet Union under Stalin.
Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939 started World War II in Europe.
Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor (1941) brought the US into the war.
lessons.try: Compare the totalitarian regimes of the 1930s.

lessons.t: The Holocaust and the End of the War
learn: In the Holocaust, Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews and millions of others, including Roma, disabled people and political opponents.
The Allies defeated Germany in May 1945 and Japan in August 1945.
The United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent future wars.
check: About ___ million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.
The United Nations was founded in...
lessons.try: Read testimony from a Holocaust survivor and reflect on why remembering matters.

learn: After WWII, the US and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers.
The "Iron Curtain" divided Europe; NATO and the Warsaw Pact formed.
The arms race created the threat of nuclear war.
check: The Cold War rivals were the US and the...
lessons.try: Map Cold War alliances in 1955.

learn: Proxy wars were fought in Korea (1950-1953) and Vietnam (1955-1975).
The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world close to nuclear war.
The Space Race saw the Soviet Sputnik (1957) and the US Moon landing (1969).
check: The Cuban Missile Crisis was in...
lessons.try: Make a timeline of Cold War events.

lessons.t: Decolonization and the End of the Cold War
learn: India gained independence in 1947 through a movement led by Mahatma Gandhi using nonviolent resistance.
Many African nations gained independence in the 1950s and 1960s, Ghana first in 1957.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989; the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
lessons.try: Research the independence of one African nation.

learn: Globalisation connects economies, cultures and people through trade, technology and travel.
It has lifted many out of poverty but also created inequality and job shifts.
Organisations like the WTO, UN and EU shape international cooperation.
check: A cost of globalisation can be...
lessons.try: Trace where items in your home were made.

learn: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set global standards.
Movements for civil rights, women's rights and democracy continue worldwide.
Global challenges include climate change, pandemics, migration and conflict.
check: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was in...
lessons.try: Choose a global challenge and research responses to it.

learn: The internet and digital technology have transformed communication and economies.
Technology raises questions about privacy, misinformation and work.
Citizens shape the future by staying informed and participating.
lessons.try: Write an essay on how one technology has changed the world since 1990.
